Elderly Health Awareness
Simple Steps for a Healthier, Safer Old Age
A Public Health Awareness Guide for Families and Communities
1. Overview
As people grow older, their bodies go through natural changes. Bones become weaker, eyesight and hearing may reduce, muscles lose strength, and the body takes longer to recover from illness. These changes are a normal part of ageing, but many problems linked to old age can be reduced or managed if families and elders themselves stay aware and take small precautions.
India's elderly population is growing steadily every year. Health authorities have recognised that older adults need special attention because they often deal with more than one health condition at the same time, such as high blood pressure, diabetes, joint pain, or heart disease. This guide explains, in simple language, the common health concerns of old age, how to prevent falls, and how to use medicines safely. It is meant for families in villages, small towns, and cities who want to care for their elders in the right way.
2. Key Practices
A. Common Age-Related Health Concerns
Joint and bone problems: Pain in knees, hips, and back is common due to weakening bones and joints. Regular gentle movement and a diet with calcium (milk, curd, green leafy vegetables) can help.
High blood pressure, diabetes, and heart disease: These are called non-communicable diseases and are very common in old age. Regular check-ups at the nearest sub-centre, PHC, or hospital help catch problems early.
Weak eyesight and hearing: Cataracts and hearing loss increase with age. Yearly eye and ear check-ups can prevent accidents and improve quality of life.
Memory and mental health: Some elders may face memory loss, confusion, loneliness, or sadness. Family time, social activity, and talking openly about feelings are important.
Weakness and poor nutrition: Loss of appetite and reduced ability to chew can lead to poor nutrition. Soft, nutritious, home-cooked food in small, frequent meals is helpful.
B. Fall Prevention
Falls are one of the most common and serious risks for elderly people. A fall that seems minor can lead to a fracture, especially of the hip, and a long recovery. Most falls happen at home and can be prevented with simple changes.
Keep floors dry, clean, and free of loose wires, mats, or clutter, especially near the bathroom and stairs.
Ensure good lighting in rooms, staircases, and passages, particularly at night.
Fix strong handrails in bathrooms and along staircases; use a non-slip mat in the bathing area.
Encourage the use of a walking stick or support if the elder feels unsteady while walking.
Ask elders to rise slowly from sitting or lying down, as sudden movement can cause dizziness.
Get eyesight, footwear, and blood pressure checked regularly, since poor vision, loose slippers, and low blood pressure are common causes of falls.
C. General Medication Safety Awareness
Older adults often take medicines for more than one condition, which increases the chance of mistakes or side effects. The following general practices support safe use of medicines, without replacing a doctor's or pharmacist's advice.
Always take medicines exactly as prescribed by a qualified doctor; never start, stop, or change a dose on your own.
Keep a simple written list or a medicine box with day and time markings to avoid missing or repeating a dose.
Inform every doctor about all the medicines the elder is already taking, including any bought without prescription.
Store medicines safely, away from direct sunlight and out of reach of children, and check expiry dates regularly.
Report any unusual symptoms after starting a new medicine, such as dizziness, drowsiness, or stomach upset, to a health worker or doctor promptly.
Avoid sharing medicines between family members, as the same symptom can have different causes and treatments.
3. Why It Matters
Small, consistent efforts in elderly care can prevent big health emergencies. A fall that leads to a hip fracture, or a medicine taken incorrectly, can turn a healthy elder into someone dependent on others for months. On the other hand, regular check-ups, a safe home environment, and careful use of medicines allow elders to stay active, independent, and mentally well for longer.
Caring for elderly family members is also a shared social responsibility. When communities and families stay informed, elders feel respected and supported rather than isolated. This directly improves not just physical health but also emotional wellbeing in old age.
4. Odisha-Specific Context
The Government of Odisha, through the Department of Health and Family Welfare and the National Health Mission Odisha, implements the National Programme for the Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE). Under this programme, geriatric clinics and dedicated elderly care services are being expanded in district hospitals and community health centres across the state, and separate queues for elderly patients have been introduced in some OPDs to reduce waiting time.
Elders and families in Odisha, particularly in rural and semi-urban areas, are encouraged to make use of nearby Health and Wellness Centres (Ayushman Bharat) for regular blood pressure, blood sugar, and general health screening, since these services are available close to home and are generally free of cost. Along with health services, central schemes such as the Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme and assistive-device support under the Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana are also available to eligible senior citizens through local administration, and can ease the financial and physical burden of old age.
5. Source Basis
This document is based on general awareness information published by recognised public health organisations. No specific data, figures, or text has been copied directly; all information has been rewritten in simple language for easy understanding.

This content is for general awareness only and does not replace professional medical advice.
